## Normative Language Convention

This document and all documents in the AI Security ABB hierarchy use the following normative language as defined by [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119):

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SHALL** | Mandatory — the requirement is an absolute obligation |
| **SHALL NOT** | Mandatory prohibition |
| **SHOULD** | Strongly recommended — deviation requires documented justification |
| **SHOULD NOT** | Strongly discouraged — deviation requires documented justification |
| **MAY** | Optional — permitted but not required |

> **Exception and Waiver Process**: Teams that cannot meet a SHALL requirement must submit a risk acceptance or waiver request through the established enterprise governance process. Waivers require documented risk justification and approval from appropriate security leadership or designated delegate. Temporary waivers must include a remediation timeline.

### Purpose Statement

This architecture vision establishes the **strategic mandate and guiding context** for Gainwell's AI Security capability framework. As AI technologies become integral to healthcare solutions—from predictive analytics for Medicaid claims to clinical decision support—the unique security risks associated with AI systems demand specialized architectural guidance that extends beyond traditional application security frameworks.

The AI Security capability is organized as a composite Architecture Building Block (ABB) — the **AI Security Reference Architecture** ([GUID-SEC-AI-ABB-1.9.01](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-ABB-1.9.01.md)) — that defines the overarching AI security domains, principles, threat landscape, risk management approach, and integration with enterprise security architecture. Six component ABBs provide detailed capability-specific security guidance:

- **AI Data Security & Privacy** ([GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md)) — Data governance, de-identification, privacy-preserving ML techniques
- **AI Model Security & Integrity** ([GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02.md)) — Adversarial robustness, model validation, theft prevention
- **AI Infrastructure & Platform Security** ([GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md)) — Secure MLOps, container security for AI, GPU/accelerator security
- **AI Application Security** ([GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-APP-2.9.04.md)) — Secure API design for AI services, LLM application security, prompt injection defense
- **AI Observability & Incident Response** ([GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-2.9.05](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-2.9.05.md)) — Model performance monitoring, adversarial detection, audit logging
- **AI Governance & Compliance** ([GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.md)) — AI risk assessments, regulatory compliance, ethics review processes
- **AI Gateway Security** ([GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GW-2.9.07.md)) *(draft)* — AI-specific enforcement plane for prompt routing, guardrail policy, token-aware rate limiting, DLP at the AI data plane, and external AI provider governance

This framework aligns with authoritative standards including **NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)**, **NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF 2.0)**, **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications**, **MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems)**, and healthcare-specific regulations including **HIPAA**.

[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#business-value]

### Business Value

Implementing this AI Security architecture delivers critical value across security, compliance, operational, and innovation dimensions:
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#key-benefits]

#### Key Benefits

- **Regulatory Compliance & Risk Management**: Demonstrates adherence to emerging AI regulations and healthcare requirements. The architecture mapping to NIST AI RMF, CSF 2.0, and HIPAA provides auditable evidence of responsible AI practices, reducing regulatory risk. As jurisdictions worldwide implement AI-specific requirements (EU AI Act, U.S. Executive Orders on AI), this framework positions Gainwell for compliance readiness.

- **Protected Healthcare Data & Patient Privacy**: AI systems in healthcare process vast amounts of Protected Health Information (PHI) and Personally Identifiable Information (PII). This architecture ensures privacy-preserving techniques (differential privacy, federated learning, secure multi-party computation) are applied where appropriate, that training data is properly de-identified and controlled, and that models cannot leak sensitive information through inference attacks. Strong data governance prevents unauthorized access and ensures HIPAA compliance throughout the AI lifecycle.

- **Model Integrity & Trustworthiness**: By implementing controls against adversarial attacks, data poisoning, and model manipulation, Gainwell can deploy AI systems with confidence in their outputs. This is critical for healthcare where incorrect predictions could impact patient care decisions, claims processing, or fraud detection. Rigorous testing, validation, and monitoring ensure models perform as intended and maintain integrity over time.

- **Operational Resilience & Reliability**: AI systems can fail in unique ways—concept drift, catastrophic forgetting, unexpected behaviors on edge cases. This architecture establishes monitoring, incident response, and failover mechanisms specific to AI systems. Continuous model performance monitoring detects degradation early, and robust MLOps practices enable rapid retraining or rollback when issues arise, maintaining service availability and reliability.

- **Intellectual Property & Competitive Advantage Protection**: Proprietary AI models, training datasets, and algorithmic innovations represent significant IP investment. The architecture includes controls for model theft prevention, secure model serving, and protection of training processes. This safeguards Gainwell's competitive differentiation in AI-enabled healthcare solutions.

- **Responsible Innovation & Ethical AI**: Beyond technical security, this framework incorporates fairness, explainability, and bias mitigation requirements. By addressing algorithmic bias that could discriminate against patient populations, ensuring transparency in AI decision-making, and implementing human oversight for critical decisions, Gainwell can innovate responsibly while maintaining stakeholder trust and avoiding reputational harm.

- **Cost Efficiency & Audit Readiness**: Proactive security reduces the cost of breaches, regulatory penalties, and rework. Structured documentation, governance, and control mappings streamline security assessments and audits. Embedding security early in AI development (shifting left) is far more cost-effective than retrofitting post-deployment.

### Target Audience

- **Primary Audience**: Enterprise architects, security architects, AI/ML engineers, data scientists, and DevSecOps teams responsible for architecting, building, securing, and operating AI/ML systems

- **Secondary Audience**: Security operations (SOC/CSIRT) teams monitoring AI systems; compliance officers ensuring regulatory adherence; privacy officers managing PHI/PII in AI contexts; risk managers assessing AI-related risks; cloud and infrastructure architects providing platforms for AI workloads

- **Stakeholders**: Senior security, privacy, technology, and data leadership; product owners of AI-enabled solutions; clients and regulators requiring assurance of secure and responsible AI practices; legal and ethics reviewers

[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#business-context]

## Business Context

Gainwell Technologies operates at the intersection of healthcare and technology, providing mission-critical Medicaid and healthcare management solutions to government agencies and health plans across the United States. As the organization embraces AI and ML technologies to drive innovation, efficiency, and improved outcomes, the security implications of these powerful systems become paramount.
page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#business-drivers]

### Business Drivers

- **AI-Driven Innovation in Healthcare**: Gainwell is leveraging AI across its solution portfolio—predictive models for claims adjudication, NLP-powered eligibility determination, fraud detection algorithms, care coordination optimization, and conversational AI for member services. These innovations promise significant value: improved accuracy, faster processing, cost reduction, and better health outcomes. However, each AI system introduces new attack surfaces and risks that traditional security controls do not fully address. Securing AI systems is essential to realizing these benefits without compromising safety or compliance.

- **Regulatory and Compliance Mandates**: Healthcare AI operates under stringent regulatory scrutiny. **HIPAA** requires safeguards for PHI in any system, including AI models that train on or process health data. The **NIST AI Risk Management Framework** provides voluntary but increasingly expected guidance for trustworthy AI. The **Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC)** and **FDA** provide oversight for clinical AI. Emerging state-level and federal AI regulations (e.g., requirements for transparency, bias testing, or impact assessments) will increasingly affect healthcare AI. Proactively aligning AI security with these frameworks positions Gainwell for current and future compliance, avoiding penalties and maintaining contracts with government clients who demand rigorous security.

  **References**:
    - [NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
    - [Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/10/30/executive-order-on-the-safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence/)

- **Adversarial Threat Landscape**: AI systems face unique threats documented in frameworks like **MITRE ATLAS** (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial Intelligence Systems). Attackers can poison training data to introduce backdoors, craft adversarial inputs that cause misclassification (e.g., evading fraud detection), steal proprietary models through inference or extraction attacks, or manipulate model outputs to cause harm (e.g., altering diagnosis recommendations). In the healthcare context, such attacks could have life-threatening consequences or enable large-scale fraud. Traditional perimeter and endpoint security are insufficient; AI-specific defenses are required.

  **References**:
    - [MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems)](https://atlas.mitre.org/)
    - [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/)

- **Data Privacy and Ethical Concerns**: AI models can inadvertently leak sensitive information. For example, membership inference attacks can determine if a specific patient's data was in a training set, or model inversion attacks can reconstruct training data from model outputs. Given Gainwell's handling of Medicaid data (often covering vulnerable populations), privacy breaches are unacceptable. Furthermore, biased or unfair AI models could discriminate against certain demographic groups (e.g., racial or socioeconomic bias in care recommendations), leading to ethical violations and legal liability. Addressing these concerns through privacy-preserving ML techniques and fairness testing is both a security and a reputational imperative.

- **Supply Chain and Dependency Risks**: Modern AI systems rely on extensive dependencies—open-source ML frameworks, pre-trained models from public repositories, third-party labeled datasets, and cloud AI platforms. Each dependency introduces risk: malicious code in libraries, backdoored pre-trained models, data leakage through third-party APIs, or compliance issues. The software supply chain for AI is complex and rapidly evolving. Establishing secure supply chain practices, vetting dependencies, and monitoring for vulnerabilities are critical to preventing compromise at the foundation of AI systems.

  **References**:
    - [NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-218.pdf)
    - [CISA AI Roadmap](https://www.cisa.gov/ai)

- **Operational Complexity and Incident Response**: AI systems require new operational paradigms. Model performance can degrade silently due to data drift, adversarial activity may manifest as subtle accuracy loss rather than obvious breaches, and incidents may involve model behavior rather than infrastructure compromise. Traditional incident response playbooks do not cover scenarios like "model suddenly biased" or "inference API abused for data extraction." Gainwell must develop AI-specific operational security practices—monitoring model behavior, detecting adversarial inputs, responding to data poisoning incidents, and safely updating models—to maintain reliability and trust.

- **Intellectual Property and Competitive Differentiation**: Gainwell invests significantly in developing proprietary AI capabilities—custom fraud detection models, NLP pipelines for clinical documentation, predictive algorithms tuned for Medicaid populations. These models and datasets represent competitive intellectual property. Protecting this IP through secure model serving, access controls, and monitoring is essential to preserving Gainwell's market position and client confidence.

## Technical Context

Gainwell's technical environment spans cloud and on-premises infrastructure, with increasing adoption of AI/ML platforms and services. AI workloads are deployed across major cloud platforms and potentially on-premises GPU clusters or edge devices for privacy-sensitive scenarios. Development teams use diverse tools for experiment tracking, model serving, and DevOps pipelines integrating AI model deployment.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#technical-environment]

### Technical Environment

- **Heterogeneous AI Stack**: AI systems at Gainwell may range from simple regression models in production pipelines to complex transformer-based large language models. Some are internally developed; others leverage third-party AI APIs for generative or specialized tasks. This diversity means security controls must be adaptable to various model types and deployment patterns rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

- **Data Landscape**: AI systems consume data from multiple sources—Electronic Health Records (EHR) systems, claims databases, member portals, provider directories, third-party health information exchanges. Data may be structured (relational databases), semi-structured (JSON logs), or unstructured (clinical notes, images). Much of this is PHI under HIPAA, requiring strict access controls, encryption, and audit logging throughout the AI lifecycle. Data for AI training is often aggregated from production systems in data lakes or warehouses where de-identification and anonymization pipelines must be enforced before use in ML.

- **Integration with Enterprise Security**: AI systems must integrate with existing enterprise security infrastructure: identity and access management (IAM) for users and service accounts, network segmentation and Zero Trust policies, centralized SIEM logging, vulnerability scanning for containerized AI workloads, and incident response workflows.

- **MLOps and CI/CD for AI**: Gainwell is adopting MLOps practices—automated training pipelines, model versioning, A/B testing of models, and continuous deployment. While this accelerates innovation, it also introduces risks: unvetted models pushed to production, training data provenance issues, lack of reproducibility. Security must be embedded in MLOps pipelines (MLSecOps), including automated security testing, model signing, and approval gates before deployment.

- **Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs)**: Given the sensitivity of healthcare data, Gainwell may employ advanced privacy-preserving techniques: **differential privacy**, **federated learning**, **homomorphic encryption**, or **secure enclaves (TEEs)** where appropriate to mitigate privacy risks while maintaining model utility.

---
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#problem-statement]

## Problem Statement

Traditional cybersecurity frameworks are insufficient for AI systems due to the unique characteristics of AI technologies: **models as attack targets**, **training data as a vulnerability**, **inference as an exploitable interface**, and **continuous learning creating dynamic risk surfaces**. The absence of a comprehensive, enterprise-wide AI security architecture creates multiple critical challenges:
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#current-state-challenges]

### Current State Challenges

- **Unmitigated Adversarial Threats**: Models can be fooled by adversarial examples, poisoned during training, or reverse-engineered. Attackers can exploit these to bypass fraud detection, manipulate clinical predictions, or steal valuable models. The MITRE ATLAS framework documents over 40 distinct adversarial techniques, yet most organizations lack defenses against them.

- **Privacy and Compliance Violations**: AI models may unintentionally leak PHI through inference attacks or be trained on insufficiently de-identified data, leading to HIPAA violations, loss of patient trust, and regulatory penalties. Research shows models can memorize and regurgitate sensitive training data.

- **Lack of Transparency and Accountability**: Without proper governance, AI systems become "black boxes" with unclear decision logic, making it difficult to audit for bias, explain outcomes to stakeholders, or respond to incidents. This undermines trust and complicates compliance with transparency requirements.

- **Operational Blind Spots**: Traditional monitoring focuses on infrastructure (CPU, memory, uptime). AI requires monitoring model accuracy, data drift, fairness metrics, and adversarial activity—capabilities not present in standard tooling. Silent model degradation can go undetected for extended periods.

- **Fragmented and Inconsistent Approaches**: Ad-hoc approaches to AI security across projects lead to gaps, duplicated effort, and inconsistent risk posture. Teams reinvent solutions, missing lessons learned. Security architects lack clear guidance on securing AI-specific components.

- **Lack of AI Security Expertise**: Traditional security teams often lack AI/ML expertise, while data science teams may not have deep security backgrounds. This creates a dangerous gap where neither team fully owns AI security, and critical threats fall through the cracks.
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#the-need-for-foundational-architecture]

### The Need for Foundational Architecture

What is required is not just tactical security controls, but a **comprehensive architectural framework** that:

1. **Establishes Strategic Direction**: Provides enterprise-wide vision, principles, and standards for AI security
2. **Creates Consistent Taxonomy**: Defines common language and domains for AI security across the organization
3. **Enables Capability Development**: Provides the structural foundation for detailed capability-specific guidance documents
4. **Integrates with Enterprise Architecture**: Ensures AI security aligns with and extends existing security architecture (Zero Trust, defense-in-depth, etc.)
5. **Supports Governance**: Provides the framework for AI security governance, risk management, and compliance programs
6. **Facilitates Knowledge Transfer**: Educates security professionals, architects, and engineers on AI-specific security considerations
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#impact-of-inaction]

### Impact of Inaction

Failing to establish this foundational AI security architecture could result in:

- **Data breaches** exposing PHI and triggering HIPAA violations with severe financial and reputational consequences
- **Model integrity failures** causing incorrect claims processing or clinical decisions with patient safety implications
- **Regulatory penalties** and loss of government contracts due to non-compliance with emerging AI regulations (EU AI Act, Executive Orders, etc.)
- **Reputational damage** from AI bias, discrimination, or privacy violations eroding client and patient trust
- **Intellectual property theft** as proprietary models and datasets are stolen, undermining competitive advantage
- **Operational disruptions** from model failures, adversarial attacks, or inability to detect/respond to AI incidents
- **Inability to scale AI adoption** as security concerns and inconsistent approaches slow innovation

### Scope of the AI Security Capability

The AI Security ABB hierarchy applies to **all AI and ML systems** developed, deployed, or operated within Gainwell's enterprise, across:

- **AI System Types**: All supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning; deep learning; generative AI/LLMs; NLP; computer vision; predictive analytics; recommender systems; anomaly detection
- **Deployment Contexts**: Cloud AI services, on-premises ML platforms, hybrid/multi-cloud, edge AI, third-party AI APIs/SaaS
- **AI Lifecycle Phases**: Data sourcing through model decommissioning
- **Use Case Domains**: Clinical support, claims processing, fraud detection, population health, care management, conversational AI, operational analytics

[strategy/guidance/security/GUID-SEC-AI-VISION-0.9.01.md#measures-of-architecture-effectiveness]

## Measures of Architecture Effectiveness

The following key performance indicators (KPIs) define measurable success criteria for the AI Security architecture. GRC teams and governance stakeholders SHALL use these measures to assess implementation progress and ongoing compliance. These metrics correspond to the governance requirements defined in [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06](Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.md).

| KPI | Target | Measurement Method | Review Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AI System Inventory Coverage** | 100% of production AI systems registered in AI inventory | Count of inventoried systems vs. known deployments | Quarterly |
| **PIA Completion Rate** | 100% of PHI-handling AI systems have completed, approved PIAs | PIA records in GRC system | On deployment; annually thereafter |
| **Governance Review Completion** | 100% of AI systems have received risk-level-appropriate governance review before production | Governance approval records | On deployment |
| **Model Adversarial Testing** | 100% of High-risk AI systems have completed adversarial robustness evaluation | Test results in model registry | Pre-deployment; annually |
| **Encryption Compliance** | 100% of AI data stores pass encryption-at-rest validation | CSPM scan results | Monthly |
| **Audit Logging Coverage** | 100% of AI inference APIs feeding audit logs to enterprise SIEM | SIEM source inventory | Quarterly |
| **Supply Chain Vetting** | 100% of pre-trained models and ML library dependencies have documented provenance and CVE scan results | Dependency scan reports in CI/CD | Per pipeline run |
| **Incident Response Readiness** | AI-specific IR playbooks exist and tested for each High-risk AI system | Playbook inventory; tabletop exercise records | Annually |
| **Fairness Monitoring Coverage** | 100% of High-risk AI systems have active production fairness monitoring | Monitoring dashboard coverage | Quarterly |
| **Third-Party BAA Compliance** | 0 PHI transmitted to third-party AI services without active BAA and HIPAA verification | DLP log review; vendor register | Quarterly |

> **Baseline**: At architecture approval, a baseline measurement SHALL be established for each KPI. Progress SHALL be reported to governance stakeholders quarterly during the implementation phase, transitioning to semi-annual reporting once the architecture reaches steady-state operation.
